 drew fresh attention this week as crude oil prices firmed and traders weighed renewed diplomacy between Washington and Tehran, keeping the largest American energy major near the front of market conversation. Movements in Brent and West Texas Intermediate rippled quickly through the shares, underscoring how tightly the company remains bound to the global barrel even as it broadens its reach across refining, chemicals, and liquefied natural gas. Rising oil prices have reshaped the mood across the wider energy complex, and Exxon Mobil sits squarely at the center of that shift. When benchmark crude climbs, the arithmetic behind an integrated major becomes more favorable across the barrel, from wellhead production to the fuels and feedstocks that leave its refineries. The recent firming followed a stretch of choppy trading, and the swings reminded market watchers how sensitive the sector remains to headlines about supply, sanctions, and shipping lanes. The diplomatic thread running through late September added another layer. Talks involving the American administration and Iranian officials fed speculation about how quickly barrels might return to seaborne trade, and that uncertainty kept a premium in the market. For a company of Exxon Mobil's scale, such macro currents matter enormously because production spans several continents and the refining network processes crude sourced from many regions. Exxon Mobil ranks among the most recognizable names in global energy, with operations that stretch from upstream drilling to downstream fuels and a sprawling chemicals arm. That breadth gives the enterprise a measure of balance, because strength in one segment can cushion softness in another. When crude weakens, refining margins sometimes widen; when crude strengthens, the upstream barrels command more in the open market. The company has spent recent years sharpening its portfolio, leaning into lower-cost barrels and higher-value products. Management has emphasized disciplined spending and a steadier cadence of project delivery, a stance that resonates with a market that has grown wary of boom-era excess. The result is an enterprise that presents itself as leaner and more deliberate than in earlier cycles. Few developments have reshaped the Exxon Mobil story more than the offshore province in Guyana, where a string of discoveries turned a small South American nation into a meaningful source of barrels. The venture has become a signature piece of the upstream engine, delivering rising volumes from deepwater fields that rank among the industry's most closely watched. Each new phase adds capacity and reinforces the company's claim to some of the lowest-cost production in its class. Alongside Guyana, the Permian Basin in the American Southwest anchors onshore output. The combination of prolific shale acreage and offshore megaprojects gives the company two very different but complementary sources of crude. That pairing has helped push production toward record levels, a point that surfaced repeatedly in market commentary through the month. Beyond crude, Exxon Mobil has leaned harder into liquefied natural gas, positioning the fuel as a bridge in a world still hungry for reliable power. Global appetite for gas has climbed as economies seek alternatives to coal and as electricity demand rises, and the company has framed its expanding gas footprint as central to how it plans to grow. Projects spanning several regions feed into that ambition, and the theme featured prominently in recent coverage of the company's direction. The push into gas reflects a broader industry pattern in which majors chase molecules that can be shipped across oceans to premium markets. For Exxon Mobil, the gas expansion complements the crude engine and offers exposure to a market that many expect to keep expanding as heavy industry and data-hungry computing lift power needs. The downstream side of the enterprise rarely grabs headlines the way offshore discoveries do, yet it forms a vital counterweight. Refineries convert crude into gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, while the chemicals business turns hydrocarbons into the building blocks of plastics and countless everyday materials. This integrated design means the company captures value at multiple points along the chain rather than depending on a single link. A temporary outage at one American refining site drew brief notice during the month, a reminder that operating a vast physical network carries mechanical and logistical challenges. Such interruptions tend to be short-lived for an operator of this scale, but they illustrate the constant work required to keep fuel moving from crude to pump. A recurring theme in the company's messaging has been restraint on spending. Rather than chasing volume at any cost, management has signaled a preference for projects that clear high bars, an approach designed to keep the enterprise resilient when prices swing. title: With Gas at $4.48 a Gallon, Here's How Much ExxonMobil Stock You Need to Buy to Fill Up Your Tank - The Motley Fool
content: ExxonMobil dividends could help offset the rising price of fuel. According to AAA data, the national average for unleaded gas is around $4.48 per gallon. This time last year, the national average price was closer to $3.16 per gallon. Diesel prices have risen even faster. On Sept. 22, AAA recorded its highest national average for diesel fuel -- $6.53 per gallon -- since it began tracking prices. Want to help offset your exposure to rising fuel prices? ExxonMobil (XOM -0.96%) dividends are a worthwhile solution. ExxonMobil currently pays a 2.54% dividend. The average fuel tank in the U.S. is around 14 gallons. At $4.48 per gallon, it costs more than $60 for the average American to fill their tank. To pay for a single tank with dividends, investors would need to own about $2,400 worth of ExxonMobil stock. Paying for your gas regularly with ExxonMobil dividends, therefore, requires a lot of capital. But there's another way to view an investment in an oil stock such as ExxonMobil. You can use potential capital appreciation as a hedge. Over the past five years, ExxonMobil stock has risen 181% in value without factoring in dividends. Crude oil prices, meanwhile, have risen by just 26% over the same time frame. While this capital appreciation doesn't directly provide you with usable cash like dividends would, investors could gradually sell off some stock to free up capital for fuel purchases. So while paying for gas with dividends alone can be difficult, using oil stocks as a hedge against rising fuel prices could be even more effective. title: What Happens To ExxonMobil Stock If Refining Profits Fade? - Trefis
content: The worry for ExxonMobil (XOM) holders is that its refineries stop earning high margins. Management said in late July that the Strait closure keeps about 3 million barrels a day of refining capacity off the market. The second quarter alone supplied $14.5 billion of the $32.8 billion ExxonMobil earned over the last twelve months. How much of that profit rests on refining, and what would you lose if its margins fell back? Three Things Could Squeeze ExxonMobil’s Refining Profits The risks come from the market, from ExxonMobil’s own plants and from European governments. On the late-July call, management said the market benefit from the disruption was real. It also said it expects a very robust refining market with very high margins to continue. That view depends on refining supply staying short. The market risk is that the shortage ends. ExxonMobil’s refinery in Joliet, Illinois, reported a power outage in mid-September. Days later, the company said floodwater had overwhelmed a pump there. Windfall taxes came up on the same call, where an analyst noted that one European country had approved them on refining. Management said ExxonMobil cancelled planned European investments the last time such a tax passed. All three risks matter only as much as refining matters to ExxonMobil’s earnings. Refining supplies about 23% of ExxonMobil’s business-line earnings, management said, up from about 9% five years ago. That business is reported as Energy Products. It is still the biggest business by sales, with revenue of $290.3 billion in 2025. The rest of the profit comes from oil and gas production, chemicals, and specialty products. So a refining fade would reach about a quarter of business-line earnings, not the whole business. The price you pay depends on which earnings you count. A price-to-earnings multiple is the share price divided by a year of earnings per share. The stock trades at 11.7 times the second quarter’s annualized earnings—a rate that reflects Q2’s unusually strong performance. If earnings instead revert to the last twelve months’ overall level, you are paying 20.7 times earnings, against 22.4 for the S&P 500. That twelve-month figure already includes the strong second quarter. So the next question is how much cash ExxonMobil has to absorb a softer year. How Much Cash Flow Does ExxonMobil Generate For A Softer Year? ExxonMobil produced $30.6 billion of free cash flow over the last twelve months. That total also includes the strong second quarter. Free cash flow is the cash left after spending on wells, plants, and equipment. ExxonMobil’s operating profit covers its interest bill 59.5 times, so debt is not where the strain would show. Past market shocks give a sense of scale, though none of them was a refining downturn. The deepest of the three recent shocks our data covers, out of five, was the 2023 regional banking crisis. From peak to trough, the shares fell 15.0%, against 6.7% for the S&P 500. A $10,000 holding would have been worth about $8,500 at the low. Neither the cash nor past falls will tell you when refining profits start to slip. You would see it first in the third-quarter report. Management said Gulf Coast refinery reliability exceeded 95% in the second quarter; a drop there would signal broad output loss. Meanwhile, any specific cost from the September problems at the Joliet, Illinois plant will also surface in that report. Europe is the next place to look. A windfall tax in a second European country would widen the tax risk. Management already calls such taxes misguided policy. On the other side, Errea Wittu, ExxonMobil’s fifth production ship for Guyana, is due to start by the end of the year. An on-time start would add oil output even if refining profits fade. None of these markers predict where margins go. They show whether a fade is starting, and what could offset it. Refining is the slice at stake, about a quarter of ExxonMobil’s business-line earnings by management’s count. ©Copyright 2026 Insight Guru Inc. All Rights Reserved. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is set to rule on five closely watched treatments in August from Moderna, Lantheus Holdings, Bristol Myers Squibb, Capricor Therapeutics and Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical. Decisions are due by August 23 at the latest on therapies ranging from an mRNA flu vaccine to a gene therapy for a rare metabolic disorder, putting biotech investors on high alert as the outcomes could drive sharp near-term moves across the sector. Moderna is seeking approval for mRNA-1010, its experimental mRNA-based seasonal flu vaccine for adults 50 and older. An FDA advisory panel already voted unanimously in favor of the shot in June, and the FDA is slated to decide on its application by August 5. The FDA initially refused to file Moderna’s application in early February 2026, citing concerns that the comparator vaccine used in the main trial did not reflect the best available care for older adults. Moderna revised its plan, and now the company is seeking a traditional approval for adults aged 50-64 and an accelerated approval for adults 65 and older. If granted accelerated approval in the patient population, Moderna will be required to conduct another study to confirm effectiveness in the group. Lantheus wants approval for MK-6240, a PET imaging agent that detects tau protein tangles in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. Doctors would use the scan to help confirm the presence of tau pathology, stage the disease, and guide treatment decisions. The FDA accepted the company’s application seeking approval in October and granted it a fast-track designation. The application is based on two late-stage trials in people with early Alzheimer’s disease. In both trials, the scan identified patients with tau pathology and ruled out people without it, to support the application. The FDA will decide on the application by August 13 at the latest. Bristol Myers Squibb is seeking approval for iberdomide, an oral drug combined with existing medicines for patients whose multiple myeloma has returned or stopped responding, by August 17. It works by helping the immune system attack cancer cells more effectively while also directly killing myeloma cells. Bristol Myers’ application was accepted by the FDA in February and granted priority review. The application relies on the large late-stage trial where iberdomide, together with Daratumumab and Dexamethasone, showed a statistically significant improvement in minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity rates compared to control arms. MRD negativity means no detectable cancer cells remain after treatment — an early sign of deep response. Capricor is seeking full approval for Deramiocel, a cell therapy aimed at heart damage caused by Duchenne muscular dystrophy. After an earlier rejection, the company submitted new data from its late-stage HOPE-3 trial to the FDA. However, in July, an advisory committee voted 9–3 against the claim that the available evidence provides substantial proof of effectiveness for treating DMD cardiomyopathy. The vote is non-binding, meaning the FDA could still approve the therapy. Ultragenyx is seeking approval for DTX401, a one-time gene therapy for glycogen storage disease type Ia, a rare inherited metabolic disorder, by August 23. People with GSDIa cannot release stored sugar from the liver, leading to dangerous drops in blood sugar (hypoglycemia) during fasting, excess glycogen buildup in the liver and kidneys, and other long-term complications. The FDA granted priority review to Ultragenyx’s application in February. There are currently no approved treatments that address the underlying cause of GSDIa. title: Every single Robert Pattinson movie, ranked - Business Insider
content: This year alone, he's appeared in "The Drama," "The Odyssey," "Primetime," and will appear in the highly anticipated "Dune: Part Three," which is scheduled for a December release. He's come a long way since the 2000s, when he appeared in two of the biggest franchises of this century: first as the minor (but pivotal) Cedric Diggory in "Harry Potter," and then as millennials' biggest heartthrob, Edward Cullen, in "Twilight." To celebrate the release of his latest film, "Primetime," on Friday, here's a look at how critics have rated Pattinson's movies throughout his career, from his film debut in 2005 to now. Based on a true story, "Queen of the Desert" follows Gertrude Bell (Nicole Kidman) as she leaves life in England behind and travels across the Middle East, forming a love affair with a British officer (James Franco) along the way. Pattinson appears as the famous archaeologist T.E. Lawrence, who was the subject of "Lawrence of Arabia." "An emotionally empty, thematically ill-defined, and listless affair. It is never able to communicate the complexity of the woman at its center," wrote Angelica Jade Bastién for RogerEbert.com. In the period drama "Little Ashes," renowned artist Salvador Dalí (Pattinson) and poet Frederic García Lorca fall in love during the pre-Spanish Civil War era. "The drawcard of Robert 'Twilight' Pattinson as Dalí is a mixed blessing for the filmmakers, given how ill-at-ease he is in the role. Javier Beltran, as Garcia Lorca, cast as the heroic center of the film, cuts a more confident figure," wrote Philippa Hawker for The Age. The first part of a two-part adaptation of "Breaking Dawn," the final novel in Stephenie Meyer's series, "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1," focuses on Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) and Edward (Pattinson) as they go from wedded bliss to chaos. "The last twenty minutes of 'Breaking Dawn' are so harrowing that it's possible to forget that most of the acting is soap-operatic (the guy who plays Carlisle is aging to look like Liberace) and the dialogue from hunger," wrote David Edelstein for New York Magazine. In the coming-of-age drama "Remember Me," Pattinson plays Tyler Hawkins, a man who struggles to connect with his father (Pierce Brosnan) following a tragic loss. He finds solace in Ally (Emilie de Ravin), but outward influences threaten the future of their relationship. This movie's lasting legacy, though, is its twist ending — even calling it a twist feels kind of icky. "Be warned, if you're vulnerable to outrageous, cringe-inducing implausibilities — not least the ludicrous stand-up row between Tyler and his father in the latter's Twin Towers boardroom — you'd best give this one a miss," Time Out's Wally Hammond wrote. "Bel Ami" is a drama about Georges Duroy (Pattinson), a clever traveler who rises through the ranks of Parisian society in the 1890s. As he goes from extreme poverty to settings of extravagant wealth, Duroy becomes entrenched in a world of lies and seduction. "The women are all elegant and intelligent, they know the ways of the world, and they know Georges' history. Why do they find him attractive? We don't, and that failure is the downfall of the film," wrote Roger Ebert. In the second installment of the popular "Twilight" book series, "The Twilight Saga: New Moon" begins with Edward (Pattinson) leaving Bella (Stewart) behind in an effort to protect her. Heartbroken, Bella grows closer to her friend Jacob (Taylor Lautner) only to discover that vampires aren't the only supernatural creatures in their small town of Forks. "If you buy into the central romance, you'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll swoon. Otherwise, the lingering glances, lip-chewing, and regular de-shirting may cause uncontrollable giggles," wrote Helen O'Hara for Empire Magazine. Upon Edward's return to Forks in "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse," Bella (Stewart) struggles to grapple with her love for him and her burgeoning attraction to Jacob (Lautner). Amid the love triangle that develops, Edward and Jacob attempt to put their feelings aside to protect Bella from a group of malevolent vampires. "I wanted 'terrible/AWESOME' and all we got was painfully terrible. I am upset," wrote Autostraddle's Alex Vega. It's the one that started it all. In the first "Twilight" film, high schooler Bella Swan (Stewart) transfers to a new school in rainy Forks, Washington, and is immediately drawn to otherworldly student Edward Cullen (Pattinson). As Bella becomes more certain that Edward is a vampire, her love for him grows as well. The New York Times' Manohla Dargis called it "a deeply sincere, outright goofy vampire romance for the hot-not-to-trot abstinence set." In the final installment of the "Twilight" franchise, Bella (Stewart) acclimates to her new life as a vampire as she and Edward (Cullen) come together to protect their supernaturally gifted daughter, Renesmee (Mackenzie Foy), whose very existence draws the unwelcome attention of the Volturi, who are looking for any excuse to take the Cullens down. "You're going to hear a lot about 'Breaking Dawn Part 2' being the best of the 'Twilight' movies. That's like saying a simple head cold is preferable to swine flu," wrote Peter Travers for Rolling Stone. Based on the novel of the same name, "Waiting for the Barbarians" is about Colonel Joll (Johnny Depp), a magistrate who starts to question his loyalty to his empire as he oversees a colonial town. Pattinson portrays Officer Mandel, a sadistic warrant officer who works for Colonel Joll. "Intermittently engrossing and always interesting, but less potent than it could have been," wrote the AP's Jocelyn Noveck. Set in the 1930s, the drama "Water for Elephants," based on the novel of the same name, follows the romance between veterinary student Jacob (Pattinson) and star circus performer Marlena (Reese Witherspoon). Together, the two share an affection for an elephant in their traveling circus that falls under their protection. "Beauty comes in all shapes and sizes, and 'Water for Elephants' finds immense pleasure in juxtaposing extreme dimensionality with budding emotion," wrote Glenn Heath Jr. for Slant Magazine. David Cronenberg's dark comedy "Maps to the Stars" tracks the unwieldy fortune of the Weiss family, headed by TV therapist Stafford Weiss (John Cusack).  Pattinson appears as Jerome Fontana, a limo driver who forms a friendship with Agatha Weiss (Mia Wasikowska), Stafford's estranged daughter. "So here's a mean, nasty little piece of work — and I have a feeling director David Cronenberg would take that as the compliment it's intended to be," wrote Flavorwire's Jason Bailey. The drama "Life" shows a snapshot look at James Dean (Dane DeHaan) through the eyes of Dennis Stock (Pattinson), the Life Magazine photographer assigned to profile him. The two men build a budding friendship as James opens up to Dennis about life in Hollywood. "Both Pattinson and DeHaan could have used more to do, but both actors put in performances that elevate the proceedings," wrote Liz Braun for The Toronto Sun. In a corrupt town filled with death and darkness, one man (Tom Holland) attempts to protect himself and his family from evil, which includes a not-so-pious preacher (Pattinson). "Don't come for sociology. Come for top actors enjoying a weekend off the leash," wrote The Irish Times' Donald Clarke. Before "Maps to the Stars," Pattinson had collaborated with director David Cronenberg in the 2012 sci-fi drama "Cosmopolis." Set in New York City in the near future, the film features Pattinson as Eric Packer, a privileged Wall Street financier who spends most of his life in his high-tech limousine, whose life is plunged into imminent danger when he sets foot in the real world. "'Cosmopolis' is exhilarating in two ways. The first is that it offers up the soothing image of a billionaire capitalist brought to heel by riots. The second is that Pattinson's work as Packer, thorough enough that it looks like natural blankness, has since turned out to be one of the earliest indications of his talent," wrote Philippa Snow for The New Statesman. "Damsel" is a modern Western with a comedic twist, featuring Pattinson as pioneer Samuel Alabaster, a man traveling across the American Frontier to reunite with his true love, Penelope (Mia Wasikowska). With Parson (David Zellner) by his side, Samuel's journey through the Wild West grows complicated in ways they never could have predicted. Pajiba's Roxana Hadadi wrote, "The Zellner Brothers, Mia Wasikowska, and Robert Pattinson team up for the delightfully weird, beautifully shot, and feminist as hell 'Damsel.'" Set 10 years after a devastating global collapse, "Rover" is a science-fiction thriller about a loner named Eric (Guy Pearce) who does his best to survive in a lawless society. After his car is stolen by thieves, Eric forces Rey (Pattinson) into helping him retrieve his prized possession at any cost. "Brutal as it is, 'The Rover' evolves into a strange kind of buddy movie. Squint and you might be watching a nihilistic 'Rain Man,'" wrote Danny Leigh for The Financial Times. In this spy film, an intelligence agent (John David Washington) goes on an epic, time-bending journey to save the world. Pattinson plays Neil, a sidekick of sorts. "Pattinson is the best thing about the movie, bringing much-needed levity and humor. When he is not on screen, the movie doesn't feel half as fun or entertaining," wrote Jacob Sarkisian for Business Insider. The historical drama "The King" tracks the accession of King Henry V of England (Timothée Chalamet) as he inherits the throne from his deceased father. Pattinson appears in the film as the Dauphin of France, an adversary who challenges the young king's authority. "Almost everything about 'The King' works brilliantly, from the casting (not least Robert Pattinson as a deliciously detestable Dauphin) to the generally cracking script by [David] Michôd and [Joel] Edgerton," wrote Brad Newsome for The Sydney Morning Herald. Pattinson costars with Jennifer Lawrence as a married couple and new parents, Jackson and Grace, who have just moved to Montana. When Grace begins experiencing severe postpartum depression, her grasp on reality slips. "No one burns as brightly as Lawrence. Left to her own devices by a pandering script, she alone draws the line where loneliness ends and freedom begins, keeping 'Die My Love' from plunging completely into its self-made inferno," wrote Salon's Coleman Spilde. In "The Drama," Pattinson plays Charlie, a museum curator who isn't sure whether he can marry his fiancée, Emma (Zendaya), after she reveals a secret from her past. The less we say about it, the better. The Atlantic's David Sims wrote, "In 'The Drama,' Pattinson embodies Charlie as the model of tame, harmless Brit charm, and the minute the actor has built his character up, he clearly takes perverse delight in unraveling him." Director Bong Joon Ho's follow-up to best picture winner "Parasite" was "Mickey 17," a satire of capitalism starring Pattinson as Mickey, a grunt worker who volunteers to sign up as an "Expendable." Mickey is sent on dangerous jobs that will almost certainly kill him, but it's fine, because he just keeps getting cloned. "I feel like it has the makings of a cult classic — a dystopian space comedy/adventure with shades of Terry Gilliam," wrote Baltimore Magazine's Max Weiss. Set in the distant future, the arthouse film "High Life" follows a crew of death-row inmates as their space program unravels at the edge of the galaxy. Pattinson holds the lead role of Monte, a former prisoner who is soon left on the ship with only his young daughter at his side. Sight & Sound's Erika Balsom wrote, "'High Life' asks us to consider the passion — and the terror — of crossing the event horizon to cast off the laws that bind us and live another day." Based on a true story, "The Lost City of Z" delves into the life of British explorer Percy Fawcett (Charlie Hunnam) and his journey into the depths of the Amazon. Pattinson appears as military officer Henry Costin, who assists in Percy's quest to procure evidence of an undiscovered civilization. Karen Han of The Daily Beast called it "an exploration epic that will leave you breathless." Pattinson became the latest actor to wear the cape and cowl to play Bruce Wayne/Batman in "The Batman," directed by Matt Reeves. In Reeves' version of the story, Bruce is a true creature of the night, and he dedicates himself to stopping the Riddler (Paul Dano), a dangerous and brilliant serial killer. "Robert Pattinson shuts all his haters up with a vulnerable and terrifying performance in Matt Reeves's 'The Batman,'" wrote Chicago Reader's Noëlle D. Lilley. Pattinson's second-to-last film of 2026 is "Primetime," in which he plays the host and creator of "To Catch a Predator," Chris Hansen. The trailer became a huge meme engine, so we can expect the movie to be too. "On a technical and performance level, you'd be hard-pressed to find a film this year as adept at taking the internal psychopathy of its fraught subject and externalizing it as 'Primetime' does," wrote The Seattle Times' Chase Hutchinson. "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" is the fourth installment in the popular "Harry Potter" fantasy series, focusing on Harry's fourth year at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Forced to contend in a magical tournament, Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) builds an unexpected friendship with Hufflepuff student and fellow champion Cedric Diggory (Pattinson). "For those like me who are outside but sympathetic to the faith, it looks like another handsomely made, good-natured and high-spirited family movie, which is dramatically stymied through being locked within school grounds," wrote The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw. Set in Europe during World War I, "The Childhood of a Leader" is a historical drama centered on the son of an American diplomat, navigating life during wartime. The dark coming-of-age story allows viewers to see France through Charles' eyes as he witnesses the signing of the Treaty of Versailles and the first glimpses of fascism in Europe. Pattinson plays an investigative journalist in the film, with a second role as an older version of the protagonist later on. Rex Reed of The Observer wrote, "'The Childhood of a Leader' is a dark and creepy work, flawed but ambitious and well worth seeing." Horror and drama in equal measure, "The Lighthouse" tells the story of two lighthouse keepers: Thomas Wake (Willem Dafoe) and Ephraim Winslow (Pattinson). The two are driven to madness and delusion as they man their lighthouse post on a remote New England island in the 1890s. "What is the opposite of a crowd-pleaser? A crowd-splitter, maybe? Whatever you call it, 'The Lighthouse' is one," wrote Chris Hewitt for The Minnesota Star Tribune. In the crime thriller "Good Time," Constantine Nikas (Pattinson) races through the nasty underbelly of New York City's criminal world in an effort to free his younger brother from jail. As Constantine desperately accrues more money to save his brother, he finds himself putting his own life on the line. Peter Howell wrote for the Toronto Star, "Pattinson makes Connie one of the best roles of his career by turning a two-bit hood into a loyal family guy driven to help his brother. John Steinbeck would recognize these characters. So would Martin Scorsese, who is thanked in the credits." One of the biggest movies of 2026 was "The Odyssey," based on Homer's epic poem. Pattinson plays one of the film's biggest antagonists, Antinous, a suitor posted up at Ithaca, just waiting for Penelope (Anne Hathaway) to give up on her husband, Odysseus (Matt Damon), ever coming home. Business Insider's Jason Guerrasio called Pattinson "perfect" in the role. Pattinson voices the titular heron in the English dub of Hayao Miyazaki's latest (and perhaps final) film. And, as you might've guessed, he goes sicko mode voicing this creepy little bird in a vocal performance that haunts three years later. "If this really is Miyazaki's final word, then it's a conclusion worthy of his legacy. At the same time, his imagination remains so vast, it feels like he could keep creating forever," wrote The Independent's Clarisse Loughrey. Note: All scores were current on the date of publication and are subject to change. Films without critical ratings were not included. Films in which Pattinson had an uncredited role were also not included.

In plain English, the stock is hovering in the middle of its recent range, which often produces choppy trading until price escapes one side of the band. The lack of a fresh MA-cross also reinforces that message. A moving-average cross is a trend-change signal, and the absence of one suggests the market has not yet committed to a new direction. The Bollinger Band structure adds another layer: the upper band is 168.68, the middle line is 162.25, and the lower band is 155.81. With price at 44% of the 20-hour range and band width at 7.9%, the chart is showing a squeeze, or tightening price action, which often precedes a larger move. Tight bands do not predict direction by themselves, but they do warn that the next swing could be sharper than recent trading. The broader range confirms that view. ExxonMobil is still below the 3-month high of 169.64 but well above the 3-month low of 134.95, which means the stock is not in a panic phase and not in a strong trend phase either. It is sitting in the middle ground where technical signals can flip quickly if volume expands. Momentum indicators are mixed, and that is the key message. The RSI at 51.4 is neutral, so the stock is neither overbought nor oversold. That usually means there is no immediate momentum exhaustion, but also no strong trend thrust. The Stochastic %K at 35.9 and %D at 22.4 are also neutral, though the lower %D line suggests the short-term bounce has not yet fully matured into a strong upside signal. The more cautionary reading comes from MACD. The MACD at 1.059 is below the signal line at 1.775, and the histogram at -0.716 is negative. That combination tells the market’s recent momentum is still weaker than its slower trend baseline. In practical terms, traders are seeing a stock that can rise on a day, but has not yet generated the internal force needed to sustain a stronger advance. The RSI and Stochastic being neutral while MACD remains negative is a classic sign of hesitation rather than conviction. Volatility is moderate, not extreme. The ATR(14) at 4.05, or 2.5% of price, suggests ExxonMobil can move enough to matter in a short session, but not in a disorderly way. Combined with the Bollinger squeeze, that points to a market coiling rather than trending aggressively. That means the recent uptick was not powered by broad participation, which weakens the significance of the gain. Still, OBV is rising, and that matters because On-Balance Volume tracks whether money is flowing into the stock over time.
